mean: extremely big in size or amount
ex: An enormous crowd gathered outside Wankhede Stadium to welcome the team home.
ex2: Ravi's grandmother cooked an enormous pot of sambar, enough for the whole street during Pongal.
note: It already means 'very big', so never say 'very enormous'. The same goes for huge, immense and tiny.

mean: extremely small
ex: Five students share a tiny room in a Kota hostel, with one ceiling fan between them.
ex2: Meera's tiny tea stall near Howrah station sells more than five hundred cups of chai every morning.
note: Don't say 'very tiny'. 'A tiny bit' is a friendly, informal way to say 'slightly'.

mean: as much as you need, or more
ex: Don't worry about the extra guests; there is plenty of biryani for everyone.
ex2: After a good monsoon, the farmers near Nashik have plenty of water for the winter crop.
note: Use 'plenty of' + noun. Alone it works too: 'Take some, we have plenty.' Not 'plenty many' or 'plenty much'.

mean: not happening or found very often
ex: A clear, starry night sky over Mumbai is rare these days.
ex2: A century by a number eleven batsman is so rare that the commentators could hardly believe it.
note: Rare means few exist or it seldom happens; scarce means less than we need. Tigers are rare; water in May is scarce.

mean: usual or normal; neither high nor low
ex: On an average weekday, the Delhi Metro carries lakhs of passengers.
ex2: An average family in Lucknow spends a large share of its monthly budget on school fees.
note: Also a maths noun: add up and divide. Calling someone's work 'average' is mild criticism: not bad, but not good.

mean: large enough to be important or noticed
ex: Building a house in Kochi costs a considerable amount, so Thomas took a home loan.
ex2: Organising the neighbourhood Durga Puja takes considerable effort, so the youth club starts planning in June.
note: Don't confuse with 'considerate', which means thoughtful about others. Considerable = large; considerate = kind.

mean: small and not very important
ex: There is a slight delay on the Western line, so the 8:10 Borivali local is running late.
ex2: Dadi has a slight fever, so she will skip the wedding and rest at home today.
note: 'Not in the slightest' means not at all. The adverb 'slightly' is a neat upgrade from 'a little bit'.

mean: not enough for what people need; hard to find
ex: In May, water is so scarce in parts of Marathwada that tankers come only once a week.
ex2: During the lockdown, masks and sanitiser were scarce in every chemist shop in Pune.
note: Usually comes after the noun: 'Jobs are scarce.' Noun: scarcity. 'Scarcely' means 'hardly': 'I could scarcely breathe.'

mean: more than enough; present in large amounts
ex: Kerala's abundant rainfall keeps its backwaters and paddy fields green for most of the year.
ex2: Mangoes are abundant in May, so prices at Crawford Market drop sharply every evening.
note: Noun: abundance, as in 'mangoes in abundance'. Opposite: scarce.

mean: more than is needed, sensible or fair
ex: The DJ's excessive volume at the sangeet left the elderly guests covering their ears.
ex2: Doctors warn that excessive screen time can hurt a child's sleep and eyesight.
note: Always a complaint, never praise. 'Too excessive' is wrong, because 'excessive' already means 'too much'.

mean: not too much and not too little; medium
ex: The weather office has forecast moderate rain in Bhopal, so carry an umbrella but don't cancel the trip.
ex2: Mr Rao's doctor said moderate exercise, like a brisk evening walk, is enough to help his heart.
note: The verb is said MOD-uh-rayt and means control or chair: 'moderate a debate'. A 'moderate' person avoids extreme views.

mean: enough for the need, but not more
ex: The panchayat promised adequate drinking water for every household before summer.
ex2: The hostel warden checked that every room had adequate light and air before the new term began.
note: It means 'just enough', so calling an essay 'adequate' is faint praise. The ending sounds like 'kwut', not 'kwait'.

mean: large in amount, size or importance
ex: Priya got a substantial raise after leading her Bengaluru team through a tough product launch.
ex2: Farmers in Punjab lost a substantial part of their wheat crop to the unseasonal hailstorm.
note: Also means solid and real: a 'substantial meal' fills you up. Different from 'substantive', which means dealing with the real issue.

mean: so small that it does not matter
ex: The extra cost of the solar panels was negligible compared with what Gurpreet saved on electricity.
ex2: The difference in price between the two phones was negligible, so Imran chose the one with the better camera.
note: Don't confuse with 'negligent', which means careless, as in a negligent driver.

mean: very small; also, at the edge rather than the centre
ex: Despite the new flyover, the improvement in traffic near Hebbal was only marginal.
ex2: Onion prices saw only a marginal drop after the new crop reached the Lasalgaon market.
note: In India, a 'marginal farmer' owns less than one hectare of land. 'Marginalised' means pushed to the edge of society.

mean: sudden, severe and having a big effect
ex: Facing heavy losses, the textile mill in Surat took drastic steps and shut two units overnight.
ex2: After his heart scare, Mr Iyer made drastic changes to his diet: no sweets, no fried snacks, no late dinners.
note: Used for actions and changes, not for amounts of things: 'a drastic cut in prices', not 'drastic money'.

mean: thinly spread; only a few here and there
ex: Beyond Jaisalmer the vegetation is sparse: a few thorny bushes and miles of sand.
ex2: Attendance at the 8 a.m. lecture was sparse; only twelve of sixty students turned up.
note: It is about how things are spread, not only how many. A sparse crowd has gaps everywhere.

mean: enough, or more than enough
ex: The exam starts at ten, so leave by eight and you'll have ample time even if the bus is late.
ex2: The new flat in Pune has ample parking, so the family's two scooters and car fit easily.
note: Goes before the noun: 'ample space', not 'space is very ample'. 'Amply clear' means more than clear enough.

mean: extremely large or great
ex: Board exam season puts immense pressure on students, and on their parents too.
ex2: Winning gold at the Asian Games brought immense joy to the wrestler's small village in Haryana.
note: Fits feelings and forces you can't measure (immense joy, immense pressure); 'enormous' suits physical size better. Never 'very immense'.

mean: growing faster and faster, as when something keeps doubling
ex: The forwarded video saw exponential growth: ten shares in a minute, a thousand in an hour, a million by night.
ex2: UPI payments have seen exponential growth, reaching street vendors, auto drivers and even temple donation boxes.
note: Often misused to mean just 'a lot' or 'fast'. Strictly, it means growth that keeps multiplying: 2, 4, 8, 16. Steady growth is not exponential.

mean: too large or too small compared with something else
ex: Grounding Arjun for a whole month over one late night felt like a disproportionate punishment.
ex2: A fine of two thousand rupees for a torn forty-rupee library book seemed disproportionate to Kiran.
note: In Indian news, a 'disproportionate assets case' means someone owns far more wealth than their known income can explain.

mean: too small in amount; barely enough
ex: On a meagre pension, Lakshmi Amma still manages to send money to her grandson in college.
ex2: The farmer's meagre harvest this year barely covered the cost of seeds and fertiliser.
note: British and Indian spelling is 'meagre'; American is 'meager'. It suggests hardship: a meagre salary barely pays the rent.

mean: very many, and of many different kinds
ex: Old Delhi's lanes are full of myriad smells: frying jalebis, attar, diesel and wet earth.
ex2: In their first year, the startup's founders juggled myriad problems: hiring, funding and an app that kept crashing.
note: Both 'myriad problems' and 'a myriad of problems' are correct; the first is shorter and neater.

mean: so small that it feels insulting
ex: After a whole season of work, the farmers were offered a paltry two rupees a kilo for their tomatoes.
ex2: After twelve years of service, the company gave Suresh a paltry farewell gift: a pen and a card.
note: Carries anger: you are saying the amount is unfairly low. 'Meagre' sounds sad; 'paltry' sounds offended.

mean: in very large amounts
ex: Ananya took copious notes in every lecture, so the whole hostel borrowed them before exams.
ex2: Rukhsana Aunty served copious helpings of sheer khurma on Eid, and nobody refused a second bowl.
note: Mostly for things that flow or pile up: notes, tears, rain, food. It sounds formal; in chat, 'loads of' works.

mean: a small amount of something good, such as sense or respect
ex: With a modicum of planning, the wedding caterers would not have run out of rotis by nine.
ex2: Even a modicum of courtesy from the bank clerk would have made Mr Das's long wait easier.
note: Nearly always 'a modicum of' + a good quality. Often used to complain: 'not even a modicum of courtesy'.

mean: very large in size, amount or importance
ex: There was a huge queue outside the passport office in Ghaziabad by seven in the morning.
ex2: Winning the inter-school quiz was a huge deal for the small government school in Dumka.
note: Huge already means very big, so say 'huge', not 'very huge'. In speech it is far more common than 'enormous'.

mean: a small number of people or things
ex: Only a handful of students stayed back for the extra class on Saturday afternoon.
ex2: Despite the rain, a handful of loyal fans waited outside Eden Gardens for autographs.
note: Use 'a handful of' + plural noun. Informally it also means a hard-to-control child: 'Their son is a real handful.'

mean: small in amount or number; not as much as you would like
ex: Seats on the Diwali special train are limited, so book your ticket the day booking opens.
ex2: With limited English, Raju's mother still managed to explain her symptoms to the doctor in Chennai.
note: It means there is a fixed, small amount. 'For a limited period' and 'limited stock' are common in shop ads.

mean: too many to count
ex: Countless pilgrims walk barefoot to Pandharpur every year for the Wari.
ex2: Ishaan rewrote his college essay countless times before he finally pressed submit.
note: Use it with plural nouns: 'countless times'. For things you cannot count, like water, say 'a great deal of'.

mean: enough for a particular need
ex: The court gave the builder sufficient time to finish the flats, but work never started.
ex2: Eight hours of sleep is sufficient for most teenagers, the school counsellor told the parents.
note: More formal than 'enough'; common in rules and letters. 'Insufficient funds' is the message you get when a payment fails.

mean: very small; as little as possible
ex: The new hospital ward was built with minimal damage to the old neem trees in the compound.
ex2: Asha packed minimal clothes for the Ladakh trip but carried plenty of sunscreen.
note: 'Minimal' means as little as possible; 'minimum' is the lowest limit allowed. Minimal damage, but minimum age 18.

mean: a situation where there is not enough of something
ex: A shortage of teachers means one teacher handles three classes at the village school near Bastar.
ex2: Every summer, a shortage of tomatoes sends prices shooting up at Azadpur mandi.
note: Say 'a shortage of water', not 'shortage in water'. 'Acute shortage' is a very common news phrase.

mean: an extra amount, more than is needed
ex: After a bumper harvest, Punjab had a surplus of wheat that the godowns could not store.
ex2: The housing society used last year's surplus to repaint the building and fix the lift.
note: The opposite is 'deficit'. It also works as an adjective: 'surplus food from the wedding went to a shelter'.

mean: large and heavy, or (of money) bigger than you would like
ex: Parking in the no-parking zone at Connaught Place earned Kunal a hefty fine.
ex2: Two porters struggled to lift Nani's hefty steel trunk onto the train at Lucknow station.
note: Slightly informal but very common in news for money: 'a hefty fine', 'a hefty salary hike'.

mean: so large or surprising that it shocks you
ex: The wedding cost a staggering forty lakh rupees, and the family is still paying off the loan.
ex2: Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver a staggering two lakh lunch boxes a day with almost no mistakes.
note: Used for numbers and amounts that amaze you. It comes from 'stagger', to walk unsteadily, as if the news knocked you sideways.

mean: the main or largest part of something
ex: The bulk of the household budget goes on rent and the children's school fees.
ex2: The opener scored the bulk of the team's runs while the middle order collapsed in Chennai.
note: 'The bulk of' means most of. 'Buy in bulk' means buy a large amount at once, often cheaper, like a year's rice.

mean: a lack of something; far too little of it
ex: The district hospital faces a dearth of specialists, so patients travel four hours to Ranchi.
ex2: There is no dearth of opinions on the family WhatsApp group, only a dearth of facts.
note: Indian newspapers love 'there is no dearth of...', meaning there is plenty. It rhymes with 'earth'.

mean: much more than is normal or reasonable
ex: The judge criticised the inordinate delay in a land case that had dragged on for twenty years.
ex2: Simran spends an inordinate amount of time choosing a filter before posting any photo.
note: Very common in Indian court reports: 'inordinate delay'. Stronger and more formal than 'too much'.

mean: very small in amount, especially money; far less than the real value
ex: The library charges a nominal fee of ten rupees a month, so even daily-wage workers can join.
ex2: On the last day of the Kolkata Book Fair, volunteers sold the leftover books at a nominal price.
note: It also means 'in name only': a nominal head has little real power. Hindi 'नाममात्र' carries both senses.

mean: a small amount, especially a little knowledge of a language
ex: After a year in Chennai, Neha picked up a smattering of Tamil, enough to bargain at the market.
ex2: Only a smattering of spectators turned up for the Ranji Trophy match on a rainy Monday.
note: Most often used for languages: 'a smattering of French'. It sounds light and modest, never insulting.

mean: far more of something than people need or will buy
ex: A glut of onions in the Nashik mandis pushed prices so low that farmers dumped their crop on the road.
ex2: A glut of engineering graduates means even good students struggle to find their first job.
note: A business and news word. A surplus is a neutral extra; a glut is a harmful excess that makes prices crash.
